meta.title: Prompt Injection Defense
meta.thesis: Prompt Injection Defense is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A RAG assistant reads untrusted documents that may contain instructions to ignore system policy. By the end, they should be able to build or review prompt-injection defense plan with isolation, filtering, and tool gating, measure malicious retrieved text fails to change system behavior, and catch the failure where the model follows an instruction embedded in a support article.

blocks.title: Why Prompt Injection Defense matters here

spans.text: Problem statement: A RAG assistant reads untrusted documents that may contain instructions to ignore system policy. The learner's job is not to memorize Prompt Injection Defense; it is to decide what to build or change, what evidence the system may use, and how to tell whether the change improved malicious retrieved text fails to change system behavior.

Running case: prompt-injection defense plan with isolation, filtering, and tool gating. We will keep this same case through the lesson so each idea has a job: frame the problem, explain the mechanism, choose a design, test the implementation, and decide what to do next.

Before reading on, predict: if the model follows an instruction embedded in a support article, where would you look first - the input, the state or data, the model boundary, the validation check, or the release process?
The lesson assumes you can learn the vocabulary, then spends its effort on integration choices, failure signals, and checks that make the idea usable in a real system.

items.text: Product framing: Prompt Injection Defense matters when it changes a user-visible decision, release gate, or operational workflow.
Engineering framing: Prompt Injection Defense matters when it changes data, state, prompts, model behavior, tools, schemas, traces, or runtime constraints.
Validation framing: the lesson is not complete until the team can measure malicious retrieved text fails to change system behavior on examples that resemble the real workload.

blocks.title: Fully worked example: prompt-injection defense plan with isolation, filtering, and tool gating

spans.text: Scenario: A RAG assistant reads untrusted documents that may contain instructions to ignore system policy. The team wants to improve malicious retrieved text fails to change system behavior, but it has already seen this failure: the model follows an instruction embedded in a support article.
Here is the worked artifact at design-review depth: concrete enough to inspect, small enough to build as a thin slice.
Complete worked artifact

items.text: Launch review: a customer-facing AI feature touches user data, external tools, or regulated decisions. The team needs a risk classification and controls before it ships.

Artifact: prompt-injection defense plan with isolation, filtering, and tool gating. It maps data flows, user harms, threat scenarios, required controls, human review, logging, and the release evidence for malicious retrieved text fails to change system behavior.
Worked output: classify the feature, identify sensitive data, block unsafe tool use, add audit logging, test a misuse case, and assign an owner for unresolved risk.

spans.text: Complete AI-assistant prompt for this artifact

Role: AI safety reviewer. Context: A RAG assistant reads untrusted documents that may contain instructions to ignore system policy. Task: complete a risk review for prompt-injection defense plan with isolation, filtering, and tool gating. Include data handled, user harm, tool risk, misuse test, mitigation, owner, and release decision. Output: {risk_category, controls, tests, unresolved_risks, owner}.
Why this is richer than a definition
The example ties Prompt Injection Defense to a specific input, output, decision, failure mode, and metric. That is the move you should repeat when applying the lesson to your own system.

spans.text: Mechanism opens the machinery behind Prompt Injection Defense. In the running case, the important question is: what exactly changes between the user's request and the final output?
Mechanism means mapping data, users, tools, threats, controls, and accountability before launch.
Two framings for the same idea

items.text: Plain framing: imagine a reviewer following a checklist. They need to see what came in, what was considered, what was rejected, and why the final answer is safe to use.
Technical framing: imagine a trace. It should expose inputs, state, external evidence, model or algorithm output, validation result, and owner for exceptions.

blocks.title: Case study: what changed after the first review

spans.text: The first prototype works on the demo path. Then a reviewer runs the uncomfortable case: the model follows an instruction embedded in a support article. The output still looks confident, which is exactly why the lesson needs a richer artifact.

The team does not restart from scratch. It adds one missing control to prompt-injection defense plan with isolation, filtering, and tool gating: a stricter input contract, better source metadata, a validation assertion, a human-review edge, a rollback trigger, or an audit log depending on where the failure appeared.

items.text: Decision made: keep the thin slice, but block release until the failure is observable and repeatable.
Evidence added: the artifact now shows the input, intermediate evidence, final output, and pass/fail reason.
Metric promoted: malicious retrieved text fails to change system behavior becomes part of the release gate instead of a dashboard someone checks later.

spans.text: Case-study takeaway: a useful Prompt Injection Defense design makes the wrong answer inspectable before it reaches users.

blocks.title: How this breaks in practice

spans.text: The failure mode to keep in view is concrete: the model follows an instruction embedded in a support article. Use it as a diagnostic lens while reading every design choice.

items.text: A policy exists in prose but is not enforced at the tool, data, or release boundary.
The system passes benign tests but follows instructions embedded in untrusted content.
Sensitive data is minimized in the app but retained in logs or traces.
The broad warning sign: malicious retrieved text fails to change system behavior gets worse even though the final answer or artifact still looks polished.

spans.text: Debugging rule: inspect the earliest place where bad evidence can enter and the latest place where validation should have stopped it.

Predict before the code: should the system answer, retrieve more evidence, block, escalate, or mark the case inconclusive when this failure appears?
